sec12-card-sec12-F08.front: At least how many feet of open roadway must remain for passing traffic when parking on a rural highway?
sec12-card-sec12-F08.expected_back: Parking on a rural highway must leave at least fifteen feet of roadway for other traffic to pass.

sec12-card-sec12-F09.front: From at least how many feet in both directions must a car parked on a rural highway be visible?
sec12-card-sec12-F09.expected_back: A vehicle parked on a rural highway must be visible from at least five hundred feet in both directions.

sec12-card-sec12-F10.front: Which vehicle lights must stay illuminated when parked along a rural highway after dark?
sec12-card-sec12-F10.expected_back: After dark, a vehicle parked on a rural highway must have its parking lights and taillights on.

sec12-card-sec12-F11.front: Which side should you exit a parked vehicle on when possible, and how if using the street side?
sec12-card-sec12-F11.expected_back: Exit on the curb side if possible; otherwise check traffic before opening the street-side door and close it promptly after leaving.

sec12-card-sec12-F12.front: What two security habits apply every time you leave a parked vehicle?
sec12-card-sec12-F12.expected_back: Do not leave the ignition key in a parked vehicle, and make locking the doors on exit a habit.

sec12-card-sec12-F13.front: What checks, signal, and curb placement precede setting your wheels for hill parking?
sec12-card-sec12-F13.expected_back: Before hill parking, check mirrors and blind spots, signal right, slow while leaving traffic and stop as far right as possible.

sec12-card-sec12-F14.front: Which way must you turn your front wheels when parking uphill next to a curb?
sec12-card-sec12-F14.expected_back: When parked uphill beside a curb, turn the wheels sharply left.

sec12-card-sec12-F15.front: Which way must you turn your front wheels when parked downhill or on any hill without a curb?
sec12-card-sec12-F15.expected_back: When parked downhill or without a curb, turn the wheels sharply right so rolling would lead away from traffic.

sec12-card-sec12-F16.front: Along with the emergency brake, which gear holds an automatic, a downhill manual, and an uphill manual on hills?
sec12-card-sec12-F16.expected_back: For hill parking, apply the emergency brake and use Park in an automatic, Reverse in a manual facing downhill, or the lowest manual gear facing uphill.

sec12-card-sec12-F17.front: What three steps apply before pulling out from a parked hill position into traffic?
sec12-card-sec12-F17.expected_back: Before leaving a parked position, signal, check mirrors and blind spots, and enter traffic only when safe.

sec12-card-sec12-R01.front: What three steps come before steering slowly into an angle or perpendicular parking stall?
sec12-card-sec12-R01.expected_back: To enter an angle or perpendicular space, choose the space, check traffic and signal before moving in slowly.

sec12-card-sec12-R02.front: How do you position and finish securing your car inside an angle or perpendicular stall?
sec12-card-sec12-R02.expected_back: Steer into the chosen space, center the vehicle, move to its front, then stop and secure it.

sec12-card-sec12-R03.front: How should you scan while beginning to back straight out of an angle or perpendicular space?
sec12-card-sec12-R03.expected_back: Before backing out of an angle or perpendicular space, check traffic in every direction and keep checking as the vehicle moves straight back.

sec12-card-sec12-R04.front: How far straight back must you roll before cranking the wheel while exiting a parking stall?
sec12-card-sec12-R04.expected_back: Continue straight back until the front bumper clears the adjacent parked vehicle before steering sharply toward the intended rearward path.

sec12-card-sec12-R05.front: What sequence completes leaving an angle or perpendicular parking space once clear?
sec12-card-sec12-R05.expected_back: After clearing the parking space, stop, select Drive and accelerate smoothly while straightening the wheels.

sec12-card-sec12-R06.front: Which three things must you keep observing throughout an entire parallel-parking maneuver?
sec12-card-sec12-R06.expected_back: While parallel parking, observe surrounding traffic, pedestrians and fixed objects throughout the maneuver.

sec12-card-sec12-R07.front: How do you signal and align alongside the forward car to begin parallel parking?
sec12-card-sec12-R07.expected_back: Begin parallel parking by checking rear traffic, slowing and signaling, then stop level with the vehicle ahead about two feet away.

sec12-card-sec12-R08.front: When do you straighten your wheels during the initial rightward reverse into a parallel space?
sec12-card-sec12-R08.expected_back: Turn right and back slowly toward the vehicle behind; when the front door passes the forward vehicle’s rear bumper, straighten and continue backing.

sec12-card-sec12-R09.front: When do you cut the wheel sharply left while parallel parking, and what must you watch?
sec12-card-sec12-R09.expected_back: Once clear of the vehicle ahead, steer sharply left while backing slowly and watch the sidewalk and vehicle behind.

sec12-card-sec12-R10.front: How do you finish positioning your car and wheels inside a flat parallel parking space?
sec12-card-sec12-R10.expected_back: Finish parallel parking by steering right toward the space center and straightening the wheels unless parked on a hill.

sec12-card-sec12-R11.front: Within how many inches of the curb and how many feet from neighboring cars should a parallel-parked car rest?
sec12-card-sec12-R11.expected_back: The final parallel-parked position should be within twelve inches of the curb or road edge and at least two feet from the parked vehicles.

sec12-card-sec12-R12.front: What three steps are required before pulling out of a parallel parking space into traffic?
sec12-card-sec12-R12.expected_back: To leave a parking space, signal and check mirrors and blind spots before pulling into traffic when safe.

sec13-card-sec13-F01.front: What step-by-step sequence comes before steering into a new lane?
sec13-card-sec13-F01.expected_back: Before a lane change, check mirrors and blind spots, identify a gap, signal and look again toward the intended lane before adjusting speed and steering over.

sec13-card-sec13-F02.expected_back: Blind spots are areas around a vehicle where obstructed views prevent mirrors showing pedestrians or vehicles.

sec13-card-sec13-F03.front: What creates permanent blind spots on a car versus temporary blind spots?
sec13-card-sec13-F03.expected_back: Vehicle design and roof pillars determine blind-spot locations, while dirty glass and glare may create temporary blind spots.

sec13-card-sec13-F04.front: What physical check catches road users hidden in blind spots before turning or changing lanes?
sec13-card-sec13-F04.expected_back: Before turning or changing lanes, briefly turn the head to check for hidden road users.

sec13-card-sec13-F05.front: Where should you avoid lingering alongside other traffic, especially commercial trucks?
sec13-card-sec13-F05.expected_back: Avoid remaining in another driver’s blind spot, especially near commercial vehicles.

sec13-card-sec13-F06.front: How does driving much faster or much slower than multilane traffic affect safety?
sec13-card-sec13-F06.expected_back: On multilane roads, driving markedly faster or slower than surrounding traffic increases multi-vehicle crash risk.

sec13-card-sec13-F07.front: What should you do instead of driving faster than surrounding vehicles and passing repeatedly?
sec13-card-sec13-F07.expected_back: Driving faster than surrounding vehicles creates repeated passing situations, so slow to the traffic pace rather than repeatedly overtake.

sec13-card-sec13-F08.front: What traffic hazards and citation can result from driving far below normal traffic speed?
sec13-card-sec13-F08.expected_back: Driving much slower than other traffic can create queues and passing conflicts and may result in an impeding-traffic ticket.

sec13-card-sec13-F09.front: What should you do when vehicles stack up behind your slower travel?
sec13-card-sec13-F09.expected_back: When vehicles queue behind, pull over only when safe to let them pass, then consider an appropriate pace or a road with lower posted speeds.

sec13-card-sec13-F10.front: What is the purpose of a highway entrance acceleration lane?
sec13-card-sec13-F10.expected_back: Use an entrance acceleration lane to approach the speed of traffic before merging.

sec13-card-sec13-F11.front: Why must you avoid driving to the end of an acceleration lane and stopping?
sec13-card-sec13-F11.expected_back: Do not use up the acceleration lane and then stop, because that removes acceleration space and may surprise following drivers.

sec13-card-sec13-F12.front: Where should you ease speed if you need to wait for a freeway merge opening?
sec13-card-sec13-F12.expected_back: If waiting for a merging gap is necessary, slow earlier on the ramp so room remains to accelerate before entry.

sec13-card-sec13-F13.front: Who holds right-of-way when entrance-ramp vehicles meet mainline roadway traffic?
sec13-card-sec13-F13.expected_back: Entering traffic must yield to vehicles already on the roadway.

sec13-card-sec13-F14.front: When an exit deceleration ramp is provided, when should you drop below highway pace?
sec13-card-sec13-F14.expected_back: When an exit ramp is available, maintain traffic pace on the main road and reduce speed after entering the ramp.

sec13-card-sec13-F15.front: How should you prepare trailing traffic before turning off a fast two-lane highway?
sec13-card-sec13-F15.expected_back: When turning off a fast two-lane road with traffic behind, avoid slowing unnecessarily early and use brief, safe brake taps before reducing speed.

sec13-card-sec13-F16.front: What advantage comes from recognizing a slow-moving vehicle well ahead?
sec13-card-sec13-F16.expected_back: Recognizing slow vehicles early allows a lane change or gradual slowing instead of a sudden stop.

sec13-card-sec13-F17.front: How do steep climbs and highway entries affect heavy trucks and low-powered small cars?
sec13-card-sec13-F17.expected_back: Large trucks and small cars may lose speed on steep or long climbs and need more time to accelerate into traffic.

sec13-card-sec13-F18.front: What typical speed and rear warning mark farm tractors, animal-drawn rigs, and road equipment?
sec13-card-sec13-F18.expected_back: Farm tractors, animal-drawn vehicles and maintenance vehicles usually travel at twenty-five miles per hour or less and generally carry a rear slow-moving emblem.

sec13-card-sec13-F19.front: On which side must you overtake slow farm or maintenance vehicles, and which side is forbidden?
sec13-card-sec13-F19.expected_back: Slow when approaching those slow vehicles and pass to the left if possible, never to their right.

sec13-card-sec13-F20.front: Why must you scan carefully for bicycles even though reflectors or lights are expected?
sec13-card-sec13-F20.expected_back: Watch carefully for bicycles even though they should have reflectors or lights, because some lack them.

sec13-card-sec13-F21.front: Why must you lower speed inside crowded areas with limited maneuvering space?
sec13-card-sec13-F21.expected_back: Reduce speed in crowded areas to preserve reaction time when movement space is limited.

sec13-card-sec13-F22.front: Which six busy or confined locations commonly call for reduced speed?
sec13-card-sec13-F22.memory_hook: Shops, lots, downtown, rush, bridges, tunnels
sec13-card-sec13-F22.expected_back: Shopping areas, parking lots, downtown streets, rush-hour traffic, narrow bridges and tunnels are places where reduced speed may be needed.

sec13-card-sec13-F23.front: What specific pedestrian risk requires alertness near schools, playgrounds, and neighborhood streets?
sec13-card-sec13-F23.expected_back: Near schools, playgrounds and residential streets, watch for children who may enter without looking.

sec13-card-sec13-F24.front: What three checks and speed adjustments apply before crossing railroad tracks?
sec13-card-sec13-F24.expected_back: Before a rail crossing, ensure no train is approaching and enough space exists to clear the crossing; slow for a rough crossing surface.

sec13-card-sec13-F25.front: Which lane is used for passing on multilane highways, and what roadside area is strictly off-limits?
sec13-card-sec13-F25.expected_back: On multilane roads, use the leftmost lane to pass slower vehicles and never pass on a shoulder, paved or unpaved.

sec13-card-sec13-F26.front: Why should you complete every pass promptly and safely?
sec13-card-sec13-F26.expected_back: Complete a pass promptly and safely to minimize time alongside another vehicle.

sec13-card-sec13-F27.front: What three checks come before signaling to pass another vehicle?
sec13-card-sec13-F27.expected_back: Before passing, check oncoming traffic, mirrors and over the shoulder for following or passing vehicles, then signal when safe.

sec13-card-sec13-F28.front: How far past an overtaken vehicle should you continue before returning to its lane?
sec13-card-sec13-F28.expected_back: Steer smoothly into the passing lane and adjust speed as needed, continuing until the whole front of the passed vehicle is visible in the rearview mirror.

sec13-card-sec13-F29.front: How should you signal, steer, and manage speed when returning to your lane after passing?
sec13-card-sec13-F29.expected_back: Signal the return and steer smoothly back while maintaining or adjusting speed as necessary.

sec13-card-sec13-F30.front: What lane and speed discipline must you keep while another driver passes you?
sec13-card-sec13-F30.expected_back: When another vehicle passes you, stay in your lane and keep a constant speed.

sec13-card-sec13-F31.front: In which five roadway situations must you never attempt to pass?
sec13-card-sec13-F31.memory_hook: Oncoming, hills curves, corners, rails, bridges
sec13-card-sec13-F31.expected_back: Do not attempt a pass with approaching oncoming traffic, a hill or curve blocking the view, at an intersection, or before a rail crossing or bridge.

sec13-card-sec13-F32.front: What three adjustments should you make whenever passing a bicycle?
sec13-card-sec13-F32.expected_back: When passing a bicycle, slow down, leave as much room as possible and account for the bicycle’s speed.

sec13-card-sec13-R01.front: At posted speeds of thirty-five miles per hour or less, how much lateral clearance is required when overtaking a bicycle?
sec13-card-sec13-R01.expected_back: When overtaking a bicycle going the same direction where the posted limit is thirty-five miles per hour or less, leave at least three feet between the vehicle’s rightmost projection and the bicycle’s left side.

sec13-card-sec13-R02.front: What minimum separation is required when passing a same-direction bicycle where posted limits exceed thirty-five miles per hour?
sec13-card-sec13-R02.expected_back: For the same-direction bicycle pass where the posted limit exceeds thirty-five miles per hour, the minimum separation is six feet.

sec13-card-sec13-R03.front: May a driver partly cross a centerline or lane divider to give a cyclist legal clearance?
sec13-card-sec13-R03.expected_back: A motorist passing a same-direction bicycle may partly cross the centerline or a same-direction lane divider only when safe.

sec13-card-sec13-R04.front: How long must you maintain required lateral separation while overtaking a bicycle?
sec13-card-sec13-R04.expected_back: Maintain the required bicycle-passing clearance until safely beyond the bicycle.

sec13-card-sec13-R05.front: What offense classification applies to violating South Dakota's bicycle-overtaking clearance statute?
sec13-card-sec13-R05.expected_back: Violating the quoted bicycle-overtaking Section thirty-two-twenty-six-twenty-six point one is a Class two misdemeanor.

sec13-card-sec13-R06.front: How do you show a patrol officer you acknowledge an enforcement traffic stop?
sec13-card-sec13-R06.expected_back: Acknowledge an officer’s enforcement stop by activating the right turn signal.

sec13-card-sec13-R07.front: Where must you pull over for a patrol stop instead of stopping in a median or opposing shoulder?
sec13-card-sec13-R07.expected_back: Move to the right shoulder as guided by the patrol vehicle rather than the center median or the opposite side of a two-lane road.

sec13-card-sec13-R08.front: Where must you stop when pulled over on a freeway, even if traveling in a left HOV lane?
sec13-card-sec13-R08.expected_back: On a freeway, move fully onto the right shoulder even from an HOV lane and pull as far away from the travel roadway as possible.

sec13-card-sec13-R09.front: What kind of stopping spot should you look for during an after-dark traffic stop?
sec13-card-sec13-R09.expected_back: After dark during an enforcement stop, look for a well-lit stopping place such as near streetlights or services.

sec13-card-sec13-R10.front: What should you do with phone calls and audio once pulled over for an enforcement stop?
sec13-card-sec13-R10.expected_back: During an enforcement stop, end the phone conversation and switch off the radio to give the officer full attention.

sec13-card-sec13-R11.front: Should you step out of your vehicle to meet the officer during a traffic stop?
sec13-card-sec13-R11.expected_back: Remain inside the vehicle unless the officer directs you to leave it.

sec13-card-sec13-R12.front: Where should the driver's and passengers' hands stay during a traffic stop?
sec13-card-sec13-R12.expected_back: Keep both the driver’s and passengers’ hands clearly visible during the stop.

sec13-card-sec13-R13.front: What does the handbook recommend if your car has tinted windows when stopped on the right shoulder?
sec13-card-sec13-R13.expected_back: If windows are tinted, the handbook recommends lowering them after stopping on the right shoulder and before the officer approaches to communicate.

sec14-card-sec14-F01.front: How should your eyes search around the vehicle instead of staring at a single spot?
sec14-card-sec14-F01.expected_back: Use a regular moving visual search ahead, beside and behind the vehicle rather than staring at one area.

sec14-card-sec14-F02.front: What driving benefit comes from looking well down your intended travel path?
sec14-card-sec14-F02.expected_back: Looking far along the intended path gives time to plan speed and position changes and may avoid emergency braking or steering.

sec14-card-sec14-F03.front: How many seconds ahead of your vehicle should you ideally scan road conditions?
sec14-card-sec14-F03.expected_back: Ideally, scan conditions twenty to thirty seconds ahead of the vehicle.

sec14-card-sec14-F04.front: How should you handle speed and lane placement around a tall truck that blocks your forward view?
sec14-card-sec14-F04.expected_back: Adjust speed and position to maintain a useful view, avoiding following so close to a large vehicle that sight distance is restricted.

sec14-card-sec14-F05.front: How does spotting traffic changes early reduce hard braking and wasted fuel?
sec14-card-sec14-F05.expected_back: Early observation permits gradual slowing or lane changes that reduce unnecessary braking and fuel use.

sec14-card-sec14-F06.front: How do early speed or lane adjustments help drivers behind you?
sec14-card-sec14-F06.expected_back: Earlier driving adjustments give following drivers more reaction time and help traffic maintain a steadier pace.

sec14-card-sec14-F07.front: Where is scanning both left and right especially critical for crossing traffic or walkers?
sec14-card-sec14-F07.expected_back: Scan both sides before vehicles or pedestrians can cross the path, particularly at intersections and rail crossings.

sec14-card-sec14-F08.front: Besides marked street corners, what everyday access points count as intersections in visual scanning?
sec14-card-sec14-F08.expected_back: An intersection includes any traffic merging or crossing point, such as a side street, driveway or parking-area entrance.

sec14-card-sec14-F09.front: When should you look left and right at an intersection, including after coming to a stop?
sec14-card-sec14-F09.expected_back: Look left and right before entering an intersection and recheck just before moving after a stop.

sec14-card-sec14-F10.front: Why must you check the far side of an intersection before pulling into it?
sec14-card-sec14-F10.expected_back: Before entering, look across the intersection to ensure the route is clear through it and a stop will not block it.

sec14-card-sec14-F11.front: What three checks belong right before turning left across oncoming lanes?
sec14-card-sec14-F11.expected_back: Before a left turn across traffic, choose a safe gap, check the receiving street for vehicles or pedestrians, then recheck oncoming traffic.

sec14-card-sec14-F12.front: Which three hazards must you scan for before making a right turn?
sec14-card-sec14-F12.expected_back: Before turning right, check traffic from the left, opposing vehicles turning left and pedestrians in the intended path.

sec14-card-sec14-F13.front: When is turning right on a steady red signal illegal?
sec14-card-sec14-F13.expected_back: A right turn on red is forbidden when a sign prohibits it.

sec14-card-sec14-F14.front: Why must you scan both ways right after your traffic signal turns green?
sec14-card-sec14-F14.expected_back: Check both directions even when other traffic faces red or a stop sign, especially just after your light becomes green.

sec14-card-sec14-F15.front: What should you do after stopping if parked cars, hedges, or buildings still hide cross-street traffic?
sec14-card-sec14-F15.expected_back: If the cross-street view remains blocked after stopping, edge forward slowly until crossing traffic becomes visible.

sec14-card-sec14-F16.front: During which six driving situations does the handbook emphasize monitoring rear traffic in your mirrors?
sec14-card-sec14-F16.expected_back: Use mirrors to monitor traffic behind, especially for lane changes, slowing, stopping, intersection entry, backing and long or steep descents.

sec14-card-sec14-F17.front: How should your mirror-checking pace change when traffic around you gets heavy?
sec14-card-sec14-F17.expected_back: Check rear traffic more frequently in heavy traffic to recognize fast-closing vehicles or close following.

sec14-card-sec14-F18.front: Where else must you use full lane-change visual checks besides normal multilane shifts?
sec14-card-sec14-F18.expected_back: Lane-change checks also apply when merging from an entrance ramp or entering from a curb or shoulder.

sec14-card-sec14-F19.front: What two things must you verify in your rear and side mirrors before changing lanes?
sec14-card-sec14-F19.expected_back: Before changing lanes, use rear and side mirrors to confirm the lane is clear and no vehicle is starting to pass.

sec14-card-sec14-F20.front: Why must you turn your head over your shoulder before moving laterally?
sec14-card-sec14-F20.expected_back: Physically look over the shoulder toward the intended movement to check near the rear corners that mirrors cannot show.

sec14-card-sec14-F21.front: Which two everyday maneuvers legally require drivers to signal?
sec14-card-sec14-F21.expected_back: Drivers must signal for turns and lane changes.

sec14-card-sec14-F22.front: How far ahead must you signal before an intersection, and how many seconds ahead is advised at higher speeds?
sec14-card-sec14-F22.expected_back: The handbook requires signaling at least one hundred feet before an intersection and advises four to five seconds of advance signal at higher speeds.

sec14-card-sec14-F23.front: What two signaling methods are recognized for communicating turns and lane changes?
sec14-card-sec14-F23.expected_back: Use an electric signal or the left arm and hand to communicate the required signal.

sec14-card-sec14-F24.front: Why must side and rear checks stay brief with your eyes snapping right back ahead?
sec14-card-sec14-F24.expected_back: Make side and rear checks brief, returning attention ahead because traffic there may stop suddenly.

sec14-card-sec14-F25.front: How should you handle blind-spot verification if one quick glance is not enough before changing lanes?
sec14-card-sec14-F25.expected_back: Recheck the blind spot just before the lane change and use several short looks when needed rather than one long look away.

sec14-card-sec14-F26.front: Which smaller road users require extra visual attention when pulling out from a curb or driveway?
sec14-card-sec14-F26.expected_back: Look for motorcycles, bicycles and pedestrians that are harder to see, especially when entering from a curb or driveway.

sec14-card-sec14-F27.front: When is checking your mirror behind you most urgent while slowing down?
sec14-card-sec14-F27.expected_back: Check behind when slowing, especially during rapid slowing or at a driveway or parking space where it may be unexpected.

sec14-card-sec14-F28.front: How can smart parking selection cut down on risky reversing maneuvers?
sec14-card-sec14-F28.expected_back: Minimize reversing when possible, such as by choosing a drive-through parking space that allows forward departure.

sec14-card-sec14-F29.front: What two visual checks must you perform before and during backing instead of trusting mirrors alone?
sec14-card-sec14-F29.expected_back: Before backing, inspect behind the vehicle before entry, then turn to look through the rear window rather than relying on mirrors alone.

sec14-card-sec14-F30.front: At what pace should you reverse, and who should assist whenever available?
sec14-card-sec14-F30.expected_back: Back slowly and use an outside helper whenever one is available.

sec14-card-sec14-R01.front: What rear hazard should you watch for in your mirrors on a long or steep downgrade?
sec14-card-sec14-R01.expected_back: On a long or steep downhill, check mirrors for vehicles gaining speed, especially large trucks or buses.

sec14-card-sec14-R02.front: Which two calendar months does the handbook spotlight for heightened deer-collision alertness?
sec14-card-sec14-R02.expected_back: The handbook highlights October and November for increased deer-crash vigilance.

sec14-card-sec14-R03.front: At what two times of day are deer most active, and what visual clue betrays them along roadsides?
sec14-card-sec14-R03.expected_back: Be especially alert for deer at dawn and dusk, scanning the roadside for reflected headlight light in their eyes.

sec14-card-sec14-R04.front: What four actions should you take right away when headlight reflections show deer eyes beside the road?
sec14-card-sec14-R04.expected_back: If deer-eye reflections appear beside the road, slow, sound the horn, prepare to stop and look for more deer.

sec14-card-sec14-R05.front: Are deer crossings limited only to open country highways and rural backroads?
sec14-card-sec14-R05.expected_back: Deer may cross at any time or place, including towns and cities rather than only rural areas.

sec14-card-sec14-R06.front: What three elements work together to make up safe speed management?
sec14-card-sec14-R06.expected_back: Safe speed management combines adjustment to road and traffic conditions, sufficient following space and compliance with speed limits.

sec14-card-sec14-R07.front: When should you shed speed for a curve so your tires track stably through the bend?
sec14-card-sec14-R07.expected_back: Slow to a safe curve speed before entering so slight, steady acceleration can be used through the curve.

sec14-card-sec14-R08.front: What three situations call for dropping your curve entry speed even lower?
sec14-card-sec14-R08.expected_back: Reduce curve speed further when traction is poor, a vehicle is ahead or the curve’s end cannot be seen.

sec14-card-sec14-R09.front: What happens to tire grip if you slam the brakes after already entering a curve?
sec14-card-sec14-R09.expected_back: Hard braking after entering a curve can break tire traction.

sec14-card-sec14-R10.front: When precipitation or ice starts, why must you drop speed right away?
sec14-card-sec14-R10.expected_back: Reduce speed at the first rain, snow, sleet or ice because reduced tire grip lengthens stopping and increases skidding risk in turns.

sec14-card-sec14-R11.front: What causes hydroplaning, and how do you help prevent it in wet weather?
sec14-card-sec14-R11.memory_hook: Slow down before water lifts tires
sec14-card-sec14-R11.expected_back: Hydroplaning occurs when the steering tires ride onto pooled water, and slowing in rain or standing-water conditions helps prevent that traction loss.

sec14-card-sec14-R12.front: What should you do when large pools of floodwater cover the road ahead?
sec14-card-sec14-R12.expected_back: Do not drive through large standing-water areas on the road; use another route around flooding.

sec14-card-sec14-R13.front: From start to finish, what travel span does total stopping distance measure?
sec14-card-sec14-R13.expected_back: Total stopping distance covers travel from recognizing a need to stop until the vehicle halts, under the stated ideal conditions.

sec14-card-sec14-R14.front: How does raising your travel speed change what is needed to bring the vehicle to a stop?
sec14-card-sec14-R14.expected_back: Higher travel speed increases the time and distance needed to stop.

sec14-card-sec14-R15.front: What does perception time measure, and how long does it average for an alert driver?
sec14-card-sec14-R15.expected_back: Perception time covers recognizing the need to stop, with the handbook giving an alert-driver average from three-quarters of a second to one second.

sec14-card-sec14-R16.front: What action happens during reaction time, and what average duration does the handbook give?
sec14-card-sec14-R16.expected_back: Reaction time covers moving from the accelerator toward braking, with the handbook giving an average from three-quarters of a second to one second.

sec14-card-sec14-R17.front: Roughly how far does braking distance alone run at fifty miles per hour on dry pavement with good brakes?
sec14-card-sec14-R17.expected_back: Braking distance covers brake action to a stop; the handbook’s example is about one hundred fifty-eight feet at fifty miles per hour on dry pavement with good brakes.

sec14-card-sec14-R18.front: Why should you maintain an open space cushion around your vehicle in traffic?
sec14-card-sec14-R18.expected_back: A space cushion around the vehicle provides room and time to respond to other road users.

sec14-card-sec14-R19.front: What minimum following interval in seconds should you keep under good conditions, and why?
sec14-card-sec14-R19.expected_back: Aim for a minimum following interval of four seconds because close following restricts forward vision and response time.

sec14-card-sec14-R20.front: How do you use a roadside object to measure your following interval in seconds?
sec14-card-sec14-R20.expected_back: Measure following time from when the preceding vehicle’s rear passes a fixed landmark until your vehicle reaches the same point.

sec14-card-sec14-R21.front: What should you do if your front bumper passes the landmark before you finish counting four seconds?
sec14-card-sec14-R21.expected_back: Reaching the landmark before counting four seconds means the interval is too short; slow and retest at another point until the minimum is met.

sec14-card-sec14-R22.front: How can you train your eyes to judge time distances more accurately down the road?
sec14-card-sec14-R22.expected_back: Practice estimating an object’s time distance and then count the actual travel seconds to check the estimate.

sec14-card-sec14-R23.front: How must your following gap change when pavement turns wet, snowy, or icy?
sec14-card-sec14-R23.expected_back: Leave more following space on slippery roads because stopping takes farther.

sec14-card-sec14-R24.front: How should you adjust speed when a trailing driver pulls out to pass you?
sec14-card-sec14-R24.expected_back: When the following driver wants to pass, slow enough to open space ahead and help the pass finish sooner.

sec14-card-sec14-R25.front: Why must you open extra following distance behind motorcycles and bicycles, especially on slick or loose surfaces?
sec14-card-sec14-R25.expected_back: Increase space behind motorcycles and bicycles to avoid a fallen rider, especially on wet, icy, gravel or metal surfaces.

sec14-card-sec14-R26.front: Behind which types of vehicles should you stay farther back because their drivers cannot easily see you?
sec14-card-sec14-R26.expected_back: Stay farther behind drivers who cannot see you, such as operators of trucks, buses, vans or towing vehicles.

sec14-card-sec14-R27.front: How far back can a large truck's rear blind spot reach?
sec14-card-sec14-R27.expected_back: The handbook says a large truck’s rear blind area can extend two hundred feet, and dropping back also improves your forward view.

sec14-card-sec14-R28.front: Why must you add extra following space when hauling heavy cargo or pulling a trailer?
sec14-card-sec14-R28.expected_back: Increase following space when carrying a heavy load or towing because the extra weight lengthens stopping.

sec14-card-sec14-R29.front: Why should you widen your forward gap at night, in bad weather, or when someone tailgates you?
sec14-card-sec14-R29.expected_back: Allow extra following room in darkness or bad weather and when another vehicle follows you closely.

sec14-card-sec14-R30.front: Why must you hold extra distance behind police cars, ambulances, and fire trucks?
sec14-card-sec14-R30.expected_back: Leave more space behind police vehicles, ambulances and fire trucks because they need room to operate.

sec14-card-sec14-R31.front: Which three vehicle types require extra following room at railroad crossings because they must stop?
sec14-card-sec14-R31.expected_back: At rail crossings, leave extra room behind vehicles that must stop, including transit buses, school buses and hazardous-material carriers.

sec14-card-sec14-R32.front: Why should you leave extra room behind the car ahead when stopping on an uphill grade?
sec14-card-sec14-R32.expected_back: When stopped on an incline, allow extra space in case the vehicle ahead rolls backward on starting.

sec15-card-sec15-F01.front: What steering escape advantage does keeping a side-space cushion provide?
sec15-card-sec15-F01.expected_back: A side-space cushion leaves room to move right or left if needed.

sec15-card-sec15-F02.front: Why should you avoid cruising right next to another vehicle in an adjacent lane?
sec15-card-sec15-F02.expected_back: Avoid staying alongside another vehicle because its blind spot and a reduced escape space can expose you to a crash.

sec15-card-sec15-F03.front: Where should you position your car relative to the centerline on two-way roads when possible?
sec15-card-sec15-F03.expected_back: Keep away from the centerline when possible to leave room from oncoming traffic.

sec15-card-sec15-F04.front: How can you help vehicles merging onto the roadway when traffic allows?
sec15-card-sec15-F04.expected_back: Help entering vehicles by changing lanes or adjusting speed when making room is possible.

sec15-card-sec15-F05.front: How should you position and time your pass around walkers and bicyclists, especially children?
sec15-card-sec15-F05.expected_back: Give pedestrians and bicyclists extra space, especially children, and wait to pass in an adjacent lane rather than remain alongside.

sec15-card-sec15-F06.front: Where within your lane should you ease when a large truck or bus passes you?
sec15-card-sec15-F06.expected_back: When a large vehicle passes, move toward the outside part of your lane to increase side clearance from it.

sec15-card-sec15-F07.front: How should you position yourself on a multilane road instead of riding beside another car?
sec15-card-sec15-F07.expected_back: On multilane roads, move ahead or fall back rather than remain beside a vehicle that may crowd your lane.

sec15-card-sec15-F08.front: Why must you hold extra clearance when driving past a line of parked cars?
sec15-card-sec15-F08.expected_back: Leave extra space beside parked cars because a person or vehicle may emerge.

sec15-card-sec15-F09.front: How should you position your car when squeezed between hazards on both sides at once?
sec15-card-sec15-F09.expected_back: When positioned between hazards, split the available space but give more room to the more dangerous side.

sec15-card-sec15-F10.front: How should you handle meeting an oncoming car and a bicyclist at the exact same spot?
sec15-card-sec15-F10.expected_back: When approaching a bicycle and oncoming traffic together, slowing until the oncoming vehicle passes can let you pass the bicycle with more room.

sec15-card-sec15-F11.front: What two habits of yours make it easier for a driver behind you to keep a safe distance?
sec15-card-sec15-F11.expected_back: A steady speed and early slowdown or turn signals help a following driver maintain a safe gap.

sec15-card-sec15-F12.front: Where should you pull over to load or unload passengers whenever possible?
sec15-card-sec15-F12.expected_back: Pick up or drop off passengers in a safe place outside traffic when possible.

sec15-card-sec15-F13.front: What should you do before backing into a parallel space when traffic approaches behind you?
sec15-card-sec15-F13.expected_back: Before parallel parking with approaching traffic behind, signal beside the space and allow following vehicles to pass first.

sec15-card-sec15-F14.front: Which lane belongs to slower traffic on multilane roads, and what if you delay cars behind you?
sec15-card-sec15-F14.expected_back: Use the rightmost lane when slower than other traffic on a multilane road and pull aside safely if you are holding vehicles up.

sec15-card-sec15-F15.front: How should you shed a tailgater on multilane versus two-lane roads?
sec15-card-sec15-F15.expected_back: If tailgated and a right lane exists, move right; otherwise wait for a clear, legal passing opportunity before reducing speed gradually.

sec15-card-sec15-F16.front: Why must you never tap or slam the brakes abruptly to warn off a tailgater?
sec15-card-sec15-F16.expected_back: Never brake abruptly to discourage a tailgater because doing so increases rear-impact risk.

sec15-card-sec15-F17.front: Why must you leave generous room when pulling in front of or maneuvering near trucks and buses?
sec15-card-sec15-F17.expected_back: Allow large trucks and buses extra room because they cannot stop as quickly as a car.

sec15-card-sec15-F18.front: Where and how many vehicles at a time should you generally overtake?
sec15-card-sec15-F18.expected_back: Pass only where signs or markings allow it and enough safe space exists, generally taking one vehicle at a time on the left.

sec15-card-sec15-F19.front: How quickly should you finish an overtake and get out of the passing lane?
sec15-card-sec15-F19.expected_back: Complete a pass promptly and return safely rather than lingering in the passing lane.

sec15-card-sec15-F20.front: About how many seconds does a fifty-five mile per hour pass take in the handbook example?
sec15-card-sec15-F20.expected_back: The handbook’s fifty-five-mile-per-hour example allows about ten seconds for passing and requires a corresponding oncoming gap and sight distance.

sec15-card-sec15-F21.front: At fifty-five miles per hour, how much total clear distance do two closing vehicles cover during a ten-second pass?
sec15-card-sec15-F21.expected_back: At fifty-five miles per hour, the handbook says each opposing vehicle travels over eight hundred feet in ten seconds, requiring over one thousand six hundred feet, about one-third mile, of combined clear distance.

sec15-card-sec15-F22.front: Why must you hold back from passing whenever an oncoming vehicle's closing gap feels uncertain?
sec15-card-sec15-F22.memory_hook: Distant cars close faster than seen
sec15-card-sec15-F22.expected_back: Faraway vehicles may appear still or slower than they are, so wait to pass when the available gap is uncertain.

sec15-card-sec15-F23.front: How much clear sightline is advised for passing, and where near hills or curves must you stay back?
sec15-card-sec15-F23.expected_back: The handbook advises at least one-third mile, about ten seconds, of visibility and no passing within that distance of a hill or curve hiding opposing traffic.

sec15-card-sec15-F24.front: Which three cross-traffic locations are off-limits for passing?
sec15-card-sec15-F24.expected_back: Do not pass where vehicles may enter or cross, including intersections, rail crossings and shopping-center entrances.

sec15-card-sec15-F25.front: How can the vehicle you are overtaking hide cross-traffic or train hazards from your view?
sec15-card-sec15-F25.expected_back: A vehicle being passed can block the view of road users or trains, and a turning driver may not expect a vehicle in the opposing lane.

sec15-card-sec15-F26.front: How does the handbook contrast car length with multi-trailer trucks to show why truck passes take longer?
sec15-card-sec15-F26.expected_back: The handbook compares a typical fifteen-foot car with a multi-trailer truck at least seventy-five feet long to explain why truck passing takes more time and clear road.

sec15-card-sec15-F27.front: What roadside or surface hazards ahead could force the car you are passing to swerve into you?
sec15-card-sec15-F27.expected_back: Before passing, look for pedestrians or cyclists, narrow lanes, ice, potholes or objects that could push another vehicle into the passing lane.

sec15-card-sec15-F28.front: What lane-return requirement must exist before starting a pass?
sec15-card-sec15-F28.expected_back: Do not pass without room to return to the normal lane, and never assume other drivers will create that room.

sec15-card-sec15-F29.front: Is passing permitted when approaching a railroad grade crossing?
sec15-card-sec15-F29.expected_back: Do not pass with a rail grade crossing ahead.

sec15-card-sec15-F30.front: What visual cue in your inside rearview mirror confirms safe separation to move back right after passing?
sec15-card-sec15-F30.expected_back: Before returning after a pass, leave enough separation and ensure both headlights of the passed vehicle appear in the rearview mirror.

sec15-card-sec15-F31.front: Which drivers and pedestrians need extra space because they may not see your vehicle?
sec15-card-sec15-F31.expected_back: Give extra space to people who may not see you, including drivers with blocked views, reversing vehicles, obscured windows and pedestrians whose vision is obstructed or who use a white cane or guide dog.

sec15-card-sec15-F32.front: Which four groups of distracted people along the roadway deserve extra space and caution?
sec15-card-sec15-F32.expected_back: Allow extra room or caution around potentially distracted delivery workers, construction workers, children and inattentive drivers.

sec15-card-sec15-F33.front: What four clues point to confused drivers or pedestrians who may make sudden unpredictable moves?
sec15-card-sec15-F33.expected_back: Potentially confused road users include unfamiliar visitors, drivers searching for signs or addresses, unexplained slow drivers and pedestrians affected by alcohol.

sec15-card-sec15-F34.front: Why must you hold clear of large trucks, buses, and wide loads, especially inside roundabouts?
sec15-card-sec15-F34.expected_back: Large trucks and buses need extra maneuvering room, including in roundabouts, and extra-wide loads need as much clearance as possible.

sec15-card-sec15-F35.front: What should you do if another driver botches a pass or lunges into a sudden lane change?
sec15-card-sec15-F35.expected_back: If another driver misjudges a pass or needs a sudden lane change, slow enough to let the driver return or merge safely rather than worsen the error.

sec15-card-sec15-F36.front: How do you separate multiple road hazards before reaching them at the same instant?
sec15-card-sec15-F36.expected_back: Separate hazards when possible by adjusting timing so they are passed one at a time.

sec15-card-sec15-F37.front: Which side gets the bigger space cushion when two hazards cannot be separated in time?
sec15-card-sec15-F37.expected_back: When simultaneous hazards cannot be separated, give the larger space cushion to the greater danger, such as an unpredictable child on a bicycle.

sec15-card-sec15-F38.front: Why should you switch on headlights in rain, snow, or fog even during daytime?
sec15-card-sec15-F38.expected_back: Headlights help others see the vehicle whenever visibility is poor, including rain, snow and fog.

sec15-card-sec15-F39.front: What two everyday triggers does the handbook recommend for turning your headlights on?
sec15-card-sec15-F39.expected_back: The handbook recommends turning on headlights when the wipers are needed and when daylight begins fading.

sec15-card-sec15-F40.front: Why are parking lamps unacceptable as a substitute for headlights while driving?
sec15-card-sec15-F40.expected_back: Use headlights rather than parking lamps when driving requires lights, because parking lamps serve parked vehicles.

sec15-card-sec15-F41.front: Why should you turn headlights on when driving away from a low rising or setting sun?
sec15-card-sec15-F41.expected_back: Use headlights when driving away from a low rising or setting sun so oncoming drivers facing glare can see the vehicle.

sec15-card-sec15-R01.front: How much farther do high beams reach at night compared with low beams when no oncoming car is near?
sec15-card-sec15-R01.memory_hook: High beams reach twice as far
sec15-card-sec15-R01.expected_back: High beams improve distant night visibility when there is no oncoming vehicle; the handbook describes the visible distance as twice that of low beams.

sec15-card-sec15-R02.front: Within how many feet of an oncoming vehicle must you dim your high beams?
sec15-card-sec15-R02.expected_back: Dim high beams within five hundred feet of an approaching vehicle.

sec15-card-sec15-R03.front: Within what following distance, or in what traffic density, must you stay on low beams?
sec15-card-sec15-R03.memory_hook: Under five hundred feet, heavy traffic
sec15-card-sec15-R03.expected_back: Use low beams when following another vehicle at less than five hundred feet or driving in heavy traffic.

sec15-card-sec15-R04.front: Which headlight beam and auxiliary lights belong in fog, falling snow, or heavy rain?
sec15-card-sec15-R04.expected_back: Use low beams in fog, snow or heavy rain because reflected high-beam light causes glare; use fitted fog lamps in those conditions too.

sec15-card-sec15-R05.front: Is it ever proper to drive with only your parking lamps switched on?
sec15-card-sec15-R05.expected_back: Never drive with only the parking lamps illuminated.

sec15-card-sec15-R06.front: What two steps should you take if an oncoming driver forgets to dim glaring high beams?
sec15-card-sec15-R06.expected_back: If an oncoming driver does not dim, briefly flash the high beams; if glare continues, look toward the right road edge until that vehicle passes.

sec15-card-sec15-R07.front: When are daytime running lamps no substitute for switching on full headlights?
sec15-card-sec15-R07.expected_back: Daytime running lamps improve daytime visibility but do not replace headlights at night or in fog, rain or snow.

sec15-card-sec15-R08.front: What reminder comes with manually running full headlights during the day on cars without daytime lamps?
sec15-card-sec15-R08.expected_back: Without daytime running lamps, manually using headlights provides similar daytime visibility, but remember to turn them off after shutting down the engine.

sec15-card-sec15-R09.front: What is the horn's core purpose, and how should you sound it when danger is not immediate?
sec15-card-sec15-R09.expected_back: Use the horn to communicate a crash risk, with a light tap when no immediate danger exists.

sec15-card-sec15-R10.front: When can a light horn tap warn a walker or cyclist, versus when must you yield quietly instead?
sec15-card-sec15-R10.expected_back: A light horn tap can warn a pedestrian or cyclist moving toward the lane, but at an intersection crossing yield instead of sounding the horn at them.

sec15-card-sec15-R11.front: Which driver mistakes justify a quick, light warning tap on the horn?
sec15-card-sec15-R11.expected_back: A light tap may warn a passed driver turning toward your lane or a driver who is inattentive or cannot see you.

sec15-card-sec15-R12.front: At what three sight-restricted terrain or city spots can a light horn tap prevent a surprise collision?
sec15-card-sec15-R12.expected_back: A light horn warning may be useful where a steep hill, sharp curve or narrow alley exit blocks the view ahead.

sec15-card-sec15-R13.front: Which two urgent emergencies call for a sharp, loud blast on the horn?
sec15-card-sec15-R13.expected_back: Use a sharp horn blast when another vehicle may hit you or when your own uncontrolled vehicle is moving toward someone.

sec15-card-sec15-R14.front: What three everyday social or emotional uses of the horn does the handbook forbid?
sec15-card-sec15-R14.expected_back: Do not use the horn to hurry a driver, criticize an error or greet a friend.

sec15-card-sec15-R15.front: Around which three road users or animals must you keep off the horn completely?
sec15-card-sec15-R15.expected_back: Do not sound the horn around blind pedestrians, animal-drawn vehicles or animals being herded on the road.

sec15-card-sec15-R16.front: How should you warn approaching traffic behind a broken-down vehicle and get assistance?
sec15-card-sec15-R16.expected_back: If a vehicle breaks down, warn others with flares or triangles behind it and contact authorities by phone if one is available.

sec15-card-sec15-R17.front: Where should you steer a troubled vehicle first, and which lights go on right away?
sec15-card-sec15-R17.expected_back: For vehicle trouble, move off the road and away from traffic when possible and activate the four-way emergency flashers.

sec15-card-sec15-R18.front: If your disabled car cannot clear the pavement completely, what terrain spots must you avoid stopping past?
sec15-card-sec15-R18.expected_back: If the disabled vehicle cannot get fully off the road, stop where it is visible rather than just past a hill or around a curve.

sec15-card-sec15-R19.front: Where should occupants wait during a breakdown, and what tire repair mistake must you never make?
sec15-card-sec15-R19.expected_back: Stand safely away from the roadway and use available warning devices; never change a tire from within a traffic lane.

sec15-card-sec15-R20.front: Besides hazard flashers, what visual distress cues tell passing patrols your parked vehicle needs help?
sec15-card-sec15-R20.expected_back: A raised hood or white cloth tied to the antenna, side mirror or door handle can signal a vehicle emergency.

sec15-card-sec15-R21.front: How should you handle driving near or overtaking through another vehicle's side-and-rear blind area?
sec15-card-sec15-R21.expected_back: Avoid another vehicle’s side-and-rear blind area by moving ahead or dropping back, and pass through that blind area promptly.

sec15-card-sec15-R22.front: Which two positions around a large truck or bus must you never linger in?
sec15-card-sec15-R22.expected_back: Do not remain directly beside or immediately behind a large truck or bus.

sec15-card-sec15-R23.front: How far ahead of the cab and behind the trailer do a large truck's blind zones reach?
sec15-card-sec15-R23.memory_hook: Twenty feet front, two hundred back
sec15-card-sec15-R23.expected_back: The handbook’s truck No Zone includes blind areas up to twenty feet in front of the cab, beside it and up to two hundred feet behind.

sec15-card-sec15-R24.front: What mirror check tells you whether a truck or bus driver can actually see your vehicle?
sec15-card-sec15-R24.expected_back: As a rule of thumb, if the truck or bus driver is not visible in the side mirror, assume your vehicle is not visible to that driver.

sec15-card-sec15-R25.front: Why must you warn surrounding drivers before slowing down or changing direction?
sec15-card-sec15-R25.expected_back: Warn other drivers before changing direction or slowing so they have time to react.

sec15-card-sec15-R26.front: Which maneuvers require turn signals, including both halves of passing, even when the road looks empty?
sec15-card-sec15-R26.expected_back: Signal before lane changes, turns, merging, parking and both the start and finish of a pass, even when nobody else is apparent.

sec15-card-sec15-R27.front: Why must you avoid signaling a hundred feet early if another driveway or street sits before your turn?
sec15-card-sec15-R27.expected_back: The handbook gives a turn-signal distance of one hundred feet but warns against signaling before an intervening street, driveway or entrance where another driver could misunderstand.

sec15-card-sec15-R28.front: When should you flip your blinker on if a car waits at an entrance just short of your turn?
sec15-card-sec15-R28.expected_back: If another vehicle may enter between you and the intended turn, pass that vehicle’s entry point before signaling the turn.

sec15-card-sec15-R29.front: What dashboard check belongs right after completing a gentle turn or lane change?
sec15-card-sec15-R29.expected_back: After a turn or lane change, confirm that the turn signal has stopped.

sec15-card-sec15-R30.front: How should you alert trailing drivers before making an unexpected slowdown or stop?
sec15-card-sec15-R30.expected_back: Slow as early as safely possible and tap the brake pedal three or four times before an unexpected slowdown or stop to warn following traffic.

sec15-card-sec15-R31.front: Which three road situations call for extra advance slowdown warnings to traffic behind you?
sec15-card-sec15-R31.expected_back: Give advance slowdown warning for a turn without a separate turn lane, parking or turning just before an intersection, or a hidden road obstruction or traffic queue.

sec15-card-sec15-R32.front: When are hand-and-arm turn signals useful even today, including which vintage vehicle cutoff date?
sec15-card-sec15-R32.expected_back: Hand signals can supplement turn lamps in bright sun or serve an antique vehicle built before July one, nineteen fifty-eight that may lack those lamps.

sec15-card-sec15-R33.front: How do you position your left arm and hand to signal a left turn?
sec15-card-sec15-R33.expected_back: For a left hand-and-arm turn signal, extend the hand straight outward.

sec15-card-sec15-R34.front: How do you hold your left arm and hand to signal a right turn?
sec15-card-sec15-R34.expected_back: For a right hand-and-arm turn signal, point the hand upward.

sec15-card-sec15-R35.front: How do you position your left arm and hand to signal slowing down or stopping?
sec15-card-sec15-R35.expected_back: For a stop or slowdown hand signal, point the hand downward.

sec16-card-sec16-F01.front: What three vehicle controls give you ways to avoid a crash or soften its impact?
sec16-card-sec16-F01.expected_back: The handbook identifies braking, steering and acceleration as options for avoiding a crash or reducing its impact.

sec16-card-sec16-F02.front: What two advantages do anti-lock brakes provide during a hard stop?
sec16-card-sec16-F02.expected_back: ABS helps the vehicle stop without skidding while preserving steering control; follow the owner’s instructions for its use.

sec16-card-sec16-F03.front: How should you work the brake pedal during an emergency stop with anti-lock brakes?
sec16-card-sec16-F03.expected_back: For the handbook’s ABS emergency-braking procedure, press the brake pedal hard and keep pressure applied.

sec16-card-sec16-F04.front: What sensations or sounds from an anti-lock brake pedal are completely normal in a hard stop?
sec16-card-sec16-F04.expected_back: An ABS pedal may vibrate or produce clicking during operation, which the handbook describes as normal.

sec16-card-sec16-F05.front: Can you steer during anti-lock braking, and where should drivers without anti-lock brakes check technique?
sec16-card-sec16-F05.expected_back: Steering remains possible while using ABS, and a vehicle without ABS requires its own manual’s braking procedure.

sec16-card-sec16-F06.front: How should your hands and eyes work when steering rapidly around a sudden road hazard?
sec16-card-sec16-F06.expected_back: To steer around a hazard, hold the wheel with both hands and aim toward the intended path while avoiding other traffic.

sec16-card-sec16-F07.front: What steering recovery comes right after clearing a hazard and before you slow down?
sec16-card-sec16-F07.expected_back: After clearing the hazard, countersteer to straighten and regain control before slowing.

sec16-card-sec16-F08.front: In what incoming-crash scenario can pressing the accelerator prevent an impact?
sec16-card-sec16-F08.expected_back: Acceleration may be needed to avoid a vehicle about to strike from the rear or side.

sec16-card-sec16-F09.front: What three driving or traction factors commonly set off a vehicle skid?
sec16-card-sec16-F09.expected_back: A skid can result from excessive speed for conditions, abrupt stopping or lost tire grip.

sec16-card-sec16-F10.front: What should your foot and eyes do the instant your vehicle begins to skid?
sec16-card-sec16-F10.expected_back: When a skid begins, release pressure on the brake or accelerator and look toward the desired path.

sec16-card-sec16-F11.front: How should you recover if your tires drop off the pavement edge onto the shoulder?
sec16-card-sec16-F11.expected_back: If the wheels leave the pavement, avoid a panic return, slow gradually and steer back only when safe.

sec16-card-sec16-F12.front: What routine habit lowers your odds of facing a sudden mechanical emergency on the road?
sec16-card-sec16-F12.expected_back: Follow the vehicle owner’s maintenance schedule to reduce malfunction risk.

sec16-card-sec16-F13.front: How must you treat an illuminated brake warning light on the dashboard?
sec16-card-sec16-F13.expected_back: The handbook warns against driving with a brake warning illuminated and treats it as a reason to investigate brake operation.

sec16-card-sec16-F14.front: How should you use the parking brake if your main service brakes fail while rolling?
sec16-card-sec16-F14.expected_back: If brakes fail while moving, the handbook directs gradual parking-brake application to avoid locking the rear wheels and readiness to release it if a skid starts.

sec16-card-sec16-F15.front: What is the handbook's next step if gradual parking-brake pressure still fails to stop you?
sec16-card-sec16-F15.expected_back: If the parking-brake response fails, the handbook next says to turn off the engine and find a safe place off the road to stop.

sec16-card-sec16-F16.front: May you limp a vehicle down the road once you discover its brakes do not work?
sec16-card-sec16-F16.expected_back: Do not continue driving a vehicle whose brakes do not work.

sec16-card-sec16-F17.front: How does a front tire blowout feel at the wheel compared with a rear tire blowout?
sec16-card-sec16-F17.expected_back: A blowout is a rapid loss of tire air; a front blowout pulls sharply toward that side, while a rear blowout may wobble, shake and pull toward it.

sec16-card-sec16-F18.front: What should your hands and right foot do immediately when a tire blows out?
sec16-card-sec16-F18.expected_back: For a blowout, hold the wheel firmly, maintain a straight path, ease off the accelerator and let speed fall gradually.

sec16-card-sec16-F19.front: Why should you stay off the brake pedal right after a blowout and let momentum bleed naturally?
sec16-card-sec16-F19.expected_back: Avoid braking during a blowout, allowing the vehicle to slow naturally and braking gently only if necessary.

sec16-card-sec16-F20.front: Where should you stop after bringing a blown tire under control, and what comes next?
sec16-card-sec16-F20.expected_back: After a blowout, leave the road at a safe location if possible, activate emergency flashers and replace the tire.

sec16-card-sec16-F21.front: What happens to the steering if the engine stalls while moving, and how should you grip?
sec16-card-sec16-F21.expected_back: If the engine stops while driving, keep a firm grip because steering may become harder but remains possible.

sec16-card-sec16-F22.front: How should you brake and position the car after the engine quits in traffic?
sec16-card-sec16-F22.expected_back: After engine failure, find an escape path, brake steadily instead of hard and pull off the road.

sec16-card-sec16-F23.front: What steps follow once you coast a stalled vehicle safely off the roadway?
sec16-card-sec16-F23.expected_back: Once stopped after engine failure, try restarting; if it fails, raise the hood, use emergency flashers and call for help.

sec16-card-sec16-F24.front: How does the handbook's stuck-accelerator emergency sequence begin?
sec16-card-sec16-F24.expected_back: The handbook’s stuck-accelerator sequence starts with switching the engine off, selecting Neutral and finding an escape path.

sec16-card-sec16-F25.front: How do you finish stopping a stuck-accelerator vehicle, and what must happen before driving again?
sec16-card-sec16-F25.expected_back: Its stuck-accelerator procedure then calls for smooth steering, gentle braking and leaving the roadway, with service-center pedal repair before driving again.

sec16-card-sec16-F26.front: What two priorities apply whenever your vehicle breaks down along a highway?
sec16-card-sec16-F26.expected_back: For a highway breakdown, make the vehicle visible and notify authorities by phone or another available device.

sec16-card-sec16-F27.front: Where should a disabled vehicle go immediately, and which warning lights belong on?
sec16-card-sec16-F27.expected_back: Move a broken-down vehicle away from traffic and activate emergency flashers.

sec16-card-sec16-F28.front: About how many feet behind a disabled vehicle does the handbook place warning flares?
sec16-card-sec16-F28.expected_back: The handbook places breakdown-warning flares about two hundred to three hundred feet behind the disabled vehicle.

sec16-card-sec16-F29.front: What should you try first if your headlights go dark at night, and what backup lights help you exit?
sec16-card-sec16-F29.expected_back: If headlights fail, try the switch several times; if that fails, use available flashers, turn signals or fog lamps and leave the road promptly.

sec16-card-sec16-R01.front: What should an uninvolved driver do when emergency crews are already working a crash scene?
sec16-card-sec16-R01.expected_back: An uninvolved driver should not stop at a crash when emergency help is already present, but should keep watching for people near the road.

sec16-card-sec16-R02.front: Why must drivers never drive toward a crash, fire, or disaster area just to watch?
sec16-card-sec16-R02.expected_back: Do not travel to a crash, fire or disaster merely to look, because spectators may block rescue vehicles.

sec16-card-sec16-R03.front: What must every crash-involved driver do immediately, including after bumping a parked car?
sec16-card-sec16-R03.expected_back: A driver involved in a crash must stop and must try to find the owner after striking a parked vehicle.

sec16-card-sec16-R04.front: When someone is hurt or killed in a crash, whom must you call and how long must you stay?
sec16-card-sec16-R04.expected_back: Notify police when anyone is injured or killed; an involved driver must not leave before police obtain the needed crash information.

sec16-card-sec16-R05.front: What three supply types does the handbook recommend carrying in an onboard emergency kit?
sec16-card-sec16-R05.expected_back: The handbook suggests carrying an emergency kit with warning flares, first-aid supplies and basic tools.

sec16-card-sec16-R12.front: Where should you stop after a crash, and what should you do if your vehicle still drives safely?
sec16-card-sec16-R12.expected_back: Stop at or near the crash site and move a drivable vehicle off the roadway to avoid blocking traffic or causing another crash.

sec16-card-sec16-R13.front: Where must you never stand or walk while dealing with a roadside crash?
sec16-card-sec16-R13.expected_back: Do not stand or walk in traffic lanes at a crash scene.

sec16-card-sec16-R14.front: What two fire-prevention steps belong around wrecked vehicles at a crash scene?
sec16-card-sec16-R14.expected_back: Turn off wrecked-vehicle ignitions and do not smoke nearby because spilled fuel may ignite.

sec16-card-sec16-R15.front: How should you treat fallen power lines lying on or beside the roadway?
sec16-card-sec16-R15.expected_back: Stay away from fallen power lines on or near the road.

sec16-card-sec16-R16.front: How do you keep oncoming motorists from plowing into an active crash site?
sec16-card-sec16-R16.expected_back: Use flares or other warning devices to keep approaching traffic from becoming involved.

sec16-card-sec16-R17.front: Whom should you summon when crash injuries occur, and what hazard must you mention on the call?
sec16-card-sec16-R17.expected_back: For injuries, call police and emergency medical or rescue help and report any fire when calling.

sec16-card-sec16-R06.front: What single piece of safety gear is the handbook's primary defense when a crash is unavoidable?
sec16-card-sec16-R06.expected_back: Lap and shoulder belts are the handbook’s primary advice for reducing injury when a collision cannot be avoided.

sec16-card-sec16-R07.front: How should your body, head, and foot prepare right before your car is struck from behind?
sec16-card-sec16-R07.expected_back: For a rear impact, press against the seatback, place the head against the restraint and prepare to brake against being pushed into another vehicle.

sec16-card-sec16-R08.front: How do seat belts help the driver survive and recover during a side-impact collision?
sec16-card-sec16-R08.expected_back: For a side impact, the handbook says belts help retain position while the driver prepares to steer or brake against another collision.

sec16-card-sec16-R09.front: Do standard front dashboard airbags protect occupants against side-impact forces in the handbook's discussion?
sec16-card-sec16-R09.expected_back: Front air bags do not provide the side-impact protection described in the handbook’s side-collision discussion.

sec16-card-sec16-R10.front: If a frontal crash cannot be avoided, how should you steer to reduce impact severity?
sec16-card-sec16-R10.expected_back: If a frontal impact is unavoidable, the handbook recommends trying for a glancing collision through steering rather than a direct head-on blow.

sec16-card-sec16-R11.front: Why must you keep belts fastened and stay ready to control the car during a frontal airbag crash?
sec16-card-sec16-R11.expected_back: The frontal-impact discussion anticipates air-bag inflation and deflation and emphasizes belt use and readiness to prevent a second crash.

sec16-card-sec16-R18.front: Under what two extreme dangers only should you move an injured crash victim?
sec16-card-sec16-R18.expected_back: Do not move an injured person unless the vehicle is burning or immediate danger of another vehicle striking makes movement necessary.

sec16-card-sec16-R19.front: Which crash victims get checked first, and which vital sign comes before bleeding?
sec16-card-sec16-R19.memory_hook: Silent victims first, breathing before blood
sec16-card-sec16-R19.expected_back: The handbook prioritizes people who are not already walking and talking, checking breathing before bleeding.

sec16-card-sec16-R20.front: What straightforward first-aid action does the handbook advise to control bleeding?
sec16-card-sec16-R20.expected_back: For bleeding, the handbook advises direct pressure on the wound using a hand or cloth.

sec16-card-sec16-R21.front: What may you give an injured crash victim to drink while waiting for paramedics?
sec16-card-sec16-R21.expected_back: Give an injured person nothing to drink, including water.

sec16-card-sec16-R22.front: How should you help prevent shock in an injured person at a crash scene?
sec16-card-sec16-R22.expected_back: Use a coat or blanket to keep an injured person warm as the handbook’s shock-prevention advice.

sec16-card-sec16-R23.front: Whose names and addresses should you gather after a collision?
sec16-card-sec16-R23.expected_back: Collect the names and addresses of everyone involved and witnesses, including injured people.

sec16-card-sec16-R24.front: What five categories of driver, vehicle, and coverage details should drivers exchange at a crash?
sec16-card-sec16-R24.expected_back: Exchange names, addresses, license numbers, vehicle plate and descriptive information, and available insurer and policy details with the other drivers.

sec16-card-sec16-R25.front: What physical details should you document on scene, and whom must you share crash info with on request?
sec16-card-sec16-R25.expected_back: Record vehicle damage and provide crash information to police or emergency officials when requested.

sec16-card-sec16-R26.front: What must you do if you cannot locate the owner after striking a parked vehicle?
sec16-card-sec16-R26.expected_back: After striking a parked vehicle, try to find the owner; if unsuccessful, leave visible contact information with the crash date and time.

sec16-card-sec16-R27.front: In what order do you notify police and your insurance company after an injury or fatal crash?
sec16-card-sec16-R27.expected_back: For an injury or death, contact police and give crash information at the time of the crash, then notify your insurer as soon as possible.

sec16-card-sec16-R28.front: Who can submit a required crash report if injuries keep the driver from filing it?
sec16-card-sec16-R28.expected_back: If injuries prevent the driver completing a crash report, another person may file it.

sec16-card-sec16-R29.front: What two steps apply if you damage unattended property and cannot find its owner?
sec16-card-sec16-R29.expected_back: After damaging unattended property without locating its owner, contact the nearest law-enforcement agency and leave a note where the owner can find it.

sec16-card-sec16-R30.front: Which five specific items must appear on the note left at damaged unattended property?
sec16-card-sec16-R30.expected_back: That unattended-property note must list contact details, driver-license and plate numbers, crash date and time, and damage.

sec16-card-sec16-R31.front: What does the unattended-property guidance advise regarding police arrival and leaving a crash scene?
sec16-card-sec16-R31.expected_back: The unattended-property section advises waiting for law enforcement and warns that leaving a crash scene is unlawful.

sec16-card-sec16-R32.front: Which three violations sit first, second, and third in the handbook's injury-and-fatal-crash table?
sec16-card-sec16-R32.expected_back: The printed injury-and-fatal-crash table ranks careless driving first, close following second and impaired driving third.

sec16-card-sec16-R33.front: Which three violations occupy fourth, fifth, and sixth place in the serious-crash ranking?
sec16-card-sec16-R33.expected_back: The same printed table places failure to stop fourth, improper turns fifth and disobeying traffic controls sixth.

sec16-card-sec16-R34.front: Which violations round out positions seven through ten in the handbook's crash-violation table?
sec16-card-sec16-R34.expected_back: The table’s remaining positions are overdriving conditions seventh, reckless driving eighth, emerging from an alley ninth and failing to report a crash tenth.

sec17-card-sec17-F01.front: What two habits reduce crash risk when sharing the road with everyone else?
sec17-card-sec17-F01.expected_back: Share the roadway courteously and communicate location and intended movements to reduce crash risk.

sec17-card-sec17-F02.front: Must you yield to pedestrians only inside painted crosswalk stripes?
sec17-card-sec17-F02.expected_back: Be ready to yield to pedestrians even outside crosswalks, and yield at intersection crossings even when unmarked.

sec17-card-sec17-F03.front: What must you do whenever a pedestrian crosses with a white cane or guide dog?
sec17-card-sec17-F03.expected_back: Always yield to visually impaired people and stop completely for a crossing pedestrian with a guide dog or white cane.

sec17-card-sec17-F04.front: Who goes first if a pedestrian is still crossing the intersection when your signal turns green?
sec17-card-sec17-F04.expected_back: Yield to pedestrians already in an intersection even when your light is green.

sec17-card-sec17-F05.front: What pedestrian responsibility remains whenever you make a legal turn on red?
sec17-card-sec17-F05.expected_back: A turn on red still requires readiness to yield to pedestrians.

sec17-card-sec17-F06.front: How must you handle approaching a parked or stopped vehicle that could hide a crossing walker?
sec17-card-sec17-F06.expected_back: Near parked or stopped vehicles, slow and do not pass until sure no pedestrian is crossing ahead of them.

sec17-card-sec17-F07.front: Where is scanning for pedestrians before reversing especially vital?
sec17-card-sec17-F07.memory_hook: Scan busy parking lots before backing
sec17-card-sec17-F07.expected_back: Check for pedestrians before backing, particularly in parking areas with many people.

sec17-card-sec17-F08.front: What hazard should you anticipate along residential streets and playgrounds?
sec17-card-sec17-F08.expected_back: In residential and playground areas, watch for children emerging between parked cars and be ready to stop, using a lower speed when appropriate.

sec17-card-sec17-F09.front: When do reduced school-zone speeds apply, and how must you respond to crossing patrols?
sec17-card-sec17-F09.expected_back: In school zones, obey the lower speed when warning lights flash or children are present, and stop or yield when crossing patrol signals it.

sec17-card-sec17-F10.front: How does South Dakota traffic guidance classify a bicycle riding on the roadway?
sec17-card-sec17-F10.expected_back: A bicycle on the roadway is a vehicle whose rider shares motorists’ rights, privileges, responsibilities and road rules.

sec17-card-sec17-F11.front: Why must drivers stay extra alert around bicyclists of varying experience?
sec17-card-sec17-F11.expected_back: Watch for cyclists because skill varies and an unpredictable rider may swerve, ignore controls or lack a night light.

sec17-card-sec17-F12.front: At which two crossing points must motorists yield to bicyclists?
sec17-card-sec17-F12.expected_back: Yield to bicyclists in intersections and where a bike path or lane crosses a road.

sec17-card-sec17-F13.front: Apart from driveway access, emergencies, official work, or police orders, what is forbidden in a bike lane?
sec17-card-sec17-F13.expected_back: Do not stop, park or drive in a designated bike lane or path except for alley or driveway access, official duties, police direction or an emergency.

sec17-card-sec17-F14.front: How should you time a turn when a bicyclist is riding through the intersection?
sec17-card-sec17-F14.expected_back: Slow and give cyclists ample space, allowing a cyclist to clear the intersection before you turn.

sec17-card-sec17-F15.front: Why must you never pull ahead of a bicyclist and brake hard?
sec17-card-sec17-F15.expected_back: Avoid abrupt slowing or stopping in front of a bicycle because a motor vehicle’s stronger brakes can create a collision risk.

sec17-card-sec17-F16.front: Why should you avoid honking right beside or behind a cyclist unless preventing a crash?
sec17-card-sec17-F16.expected_back: Avoid sounding the horn close to a cyclist unless needed to avert a crash, because startling the rider may cause a swerve.

sec17-card-sec17-F17.front: Which riders are especially prone to rolling off a sidewalk directly into your travel lane?
sec17-card-sec17-F17.expected_back: Watch for cyclists entering the lane, especially children moving from a sidewalk into the road.

sec17-card-sec17-F18.front: What turning mistake across a bicyclist's travel line must drivers never commit?
sec17-card-sec17-F18.expected_back: Do not turn sharply across a cyclist’s path or force the cyclist off the road.

sec17-card-sec17-F19.front: Even though cyclists must ride with traffic, where should your eyes still look for them?
sec17-card-sec17-F19.expected_back: Although cyclists must travel with traffic, look for riders anywhere on the roadway.

sec17-card-sec17-F20.front: Why do wet, sandy, or gravel-strewn roads demand extra space around bicyclists?
sec17-card-sec17-F20.expected_back: Use extra care around cyclists on wet, sandy or gravel-covered roads because those surfaces affect bicycles more strongly.

sec17-card-sec17-F21.front: Besides hand signals, what rider movement warns that a cyclist plans to turn or shift lanes?
sec17-card-sec17-F21.expected_back: Cyclists signal turns and stops by hand, but conditions may require both hands on the bars, so also watch head or shoulder looks for intent.

sec17-card-sec17-F22.front: What check is mandatory before swinging open the street-side door of a parked car?
sec17-card-sec17-F22.expected_back: Before opening a street-parked vehicle’s door, check beside and behind for bicycles.

sec17-card-sec17-F23.front: Where is checking for approaching bicycles before backing out especially critical?
sec17-card-sec17-F23.expected_back: Check for bicycles before backing, particularly near schools and homes.

sec17-card-sec17-F24.front: How much side clearance must you give a bicycle when passing where the limit is thirty-five miles per hour or lower?
sec17-card-sec17-F24.expected_back: For a same-direction bicycle pass at a posted limit of thirty-five miles per hour or less, allow at least three feet from the vehicle’s right side including projections to the bicycle’s left side.

sec17-card-sec17-F25.front: What minimum passing clearance applies around a bicycle when the posted speed limit exceeds thirty-five miles per hour?
sec17-card-sec17-F25.expected_back: For that bicycle pass above a posted thirty-five-mile-per-hour limit, allow a minimum of six feet.

sec17-card-sec17-F26.front: May you straddle a centerline or lane stripe to pass a bicycle safely, and how long must separation hold?
sec17-card-sec17-F26.expected_back: A safe bicycle overtake may partly cross the centerline or a same-direction lane line, and the required separation must last until safely past.

sec17-card-sec17-F27.front: What misdemeanor level does South Dakota statute assign to violating the bicycle-passing clearance law?
sec17-card-sec17-F27.expected_back: The quoted Section thirty-two-twenty-six-twenty-six point one classifies a bicycle-passing violation as a Class two misdemeanor.

sec17-card-sec17-F28.front: How much lane width belongs to a motorcycle compared with a passenger car?
sec17-card-sec17-F28.expected_back: A motorcycle has the same road rights and responsibilities as another driver and must receive a full lane width rather than a shared lane.

sec17-card-sec17-F29.front: Where must you look carefully for narrow motorcycles, especially right before turning left?
sec17-card-sec17-F29.expected_back: Check mirrors and blind spots for hard-to-see motorcycles and scan front and sides before a left turn.

sec17-card-sec17-F30.front: Why must you wait before pulling out in front of a motorcycle with a flashing turn signal?
sec17-card-sec17-F30.expected_back: Do not assume a flashing motorcycle signal means an imminent turn, because it may not cancel automatically; wait to confirm the rider’s action.

sec17-card-sec17-F31.front: How many seconds behind a motorcycle should you stay on dry pavement, and what about rain?
sec17-card-sec17-F31.expected_back: Follow a motorcycle by at least four seconds and allow more time in wet conditions.
